title: A life insurance payout can sit in probate for months — writing the policy 'in trust' usually avoids that
excerpt: Without being written in trust, a life insurance payout typically becomes part of the estate — which can mean waiting for probate and, depending on the estate's value, inheritance tax.
body: Choosing between level term, decreasing term and whole of life gets most of the attention when people compare life insurance — understandably, since it decides how much cover you get and for how long. But there's a separate decision that affects what happens to the payout itself, and it costs nothing extra: whether the policy is written 'in trust'.

Left as a standard policy, a payout is usually treated as part of your estate when you die. That typically means it can't be released until probate is granted, which can take months, and — depending on the total value of the estate — it can also be counted towards inheritance tax.

Writing the same policy in trust changes both of those. The payout is directed straight to the people you've named as beneficiaries, generally bypassing probate, and it usually sits outside the estate for inheritance tax purposes. For a policy meant to replace income or clear a mortgage quickly after a death, the speed difference alone is often the point.

Setting one up is normally a form completed alongside the policy application, at no extra premium — insurers typically offer a standard trust template alongside more flexible options. The trade-off is that it fixes who the beneficiaries are according to the trust's terms, so it's worth revisiting after a major life change like a divorce or a new child, in the same way you'd review the cover amount itself.

It's a small piece of paperwork sitting next to a much bigger decision, which is probably why it gets skipped — but for a policy that exists specifically to pay out quickly when it's needed most, it's worth treating as part of the same decision, not an optional extra.
